name: Chin tuck trainer
lead: A chin tuck trainer is a device, commonly an inflatable pad, strap or resistance band, that provides feedback or load during chin-tuck exercises, also known as craniocervical flexion. The exercise draws the head back over the shoulders by engaging the deep neck flexors and stretching the short extensors at the base of the skull. In appearance communities it is used to address forward head posture, which they associate with a protruding chin and a weaker-looking jawline in profile photographs.

Forward head posture, sometimes called text neck or tech neck, is commonly assessed by the craniovertebral angle, with values below about 50 degrees treated as indicating the posture.[1] Meta-analyses of therapeutic exercise for forward head posture report changes in the craniovertebral angle, with more variable effects on pain.[2][3] These reviews concern exercise programmes in general, not trainer devices specifically, and chin tucks can be performed with no equipment.

paras: Chin tuck trainers are small and inexpensive. One common form is an inflatable pad placed between the chin and chest or behind the head, against which the user tucks to hold a position. Another form is a strap or band that creates resistance against the chin or head. A related use of the same movement, chin tuck against resistance (CTAR), employs a ball or device under the chin and is studied in speech and swallowing rehabilitation, which is a separate clinical context from posture.[4][5]

According to a Grokipedia article on forward head posture, the posture involves a forward translation of the head with shortening and overactivity of the suboccipital muscles, the sternocleidomastoid and upper trapezius, alongside weakness of deep flexors such as the longus colli and capitis.[1] Chin-tuck exercise is intended to activate those deep flexors and to retract the head. The device supplies feedback about the position or adds resistance.

A 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of Manipulative and Physiological Therapeutics included seven randomised trials with 627 participants with forward head posture. It reported significant pooled effects of corrective exercise on craniovertebral angle and on pain, no significant effect on cranial angle, and graded the evidence for changing craniovertebral angle as strong and the evidence for pain as moderate.[2] A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders examined therapeutic exercises for forward head posture, rounded shoulders and hyperkyphosis in upper crossed syndrome across 22 studies.[3]

Randomised trials have tested added components. A 2022 trial examined adding scapular stabilisation to postural correction exercises in symptomatic forward head posture,[6] a 2024 trial of 60 participants evaluated a postural correction programme with scapular stabilisation and kinesiotaping on craniovertebral angle, scapular position and grip strength,[7] and a 2017 trial compared upper thoracic mobilisation with upper cervical mobilisation and stabilisation exercises.[8] These exercise-programme studies do not isolate the contribution of a trainer device, and posture changes with exercise are described as requiring repeated practice.

A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 cross-sectional studies examined the relation between forward head posture and neck pain, reporting a significant difference in head posture between asymptomatic and neck-pain groups in adults but not in adolescents.[9] This work concerns pain and not facial appearance. No study cited here evaluates whether correcting forward head posture changes the apparent jawline or chin, although proponents describe such changes in profile photographs.

Chin-tuck exercise is generally considered low-risk, but repeated or forceful tucks can produce neck muscle soreness or headache in some people, and users with neck injury, cervical disc problems or dizziness are generally advised to seek clinical guidance. A 2022 review discusses relationships among suboccipital muscles, forward head posture and cervicogenic dizziness.[10]

In posture and jawline discussions, chin tucks are presented as a free exercise that improves the neck-to-chin angle, and trainers are presented as aids for feedback or load. Because the movement can be performed without equipment, the device is commonly described in comparisons as a convenience rather than a requirement.

No studies found testing chin tuck trainer devices for appearance. Related research includes meta-analyses of therapeutic exercise for forward head posture,[2][3] randomised trials of postural correction programmes,[6][7][8] a systematic review of the link between forward head posture and neck pain,[9] and systematic reviews of chin tuck against resistance for swallowing rehabilitation after stroke, a different clinical use.[4][5]

In the swallowing literature, a 2022 meta-analysis of nine studies with 548 stroke survivors found that chin tuck against resistance improved swallowing safety and oral intake compared with no exercise.[5]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, chin tucks and forward head posture are discussed both as a free way to improve profile appearance and as a possible source of problems, with some members questioning whether correction matters or helps. [11][12][13]

claims.claim: The McKenzie chin tuck can cause neck hyperflexion and damage the spine, discs and occipital muscles.
claims.believers: An original poster on looksmax.org argues that the chin tuck promoted by Mike Mew rotates the head into hyperflexion and, if held for long periods, could damage discs and cranio-cervical muscles; a reply in the thread calls this fear mongering and says chin tucks combined with face pulls strengthen the occipital region. [11]
claims.experts: A review of therapeutic exercise reports effects on craniovertebral angle and pain, and chin-tuck exercise is generally described as low-risk, with muscle soreness or headache in some people and guidance to seek clinical advice with neck injury, disc problems or dizziness. [2][10] None of the cited studies examined injury from prolonged or forceful chin tucks.

claims.claim: Forward head posture is common among models and actors, so correcting it may be unnecessary.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster notes that many models and actors have forward head posture and asks whether correcting it is a cope; a reply says they may pose differently for photographs than they walk day to day. [12]
claims.experts: A 2019 review describes forward head posture as the most common cervical postural fault, found at different severities in almost all populations. [9] No study cited here evaluates how head posture affects perceived attractiveness.

claims.claim: Forward head posture during adolescence may contribute to maxillary forward growth.
claims.believers: A reply in a looksmax.org thread says the member had forward head posture through their teens from heavy gaming and has a forward-grown maxilla that other family members lack, and wonders whether the two are related. [12]
claims.experts: No study cited in this article examines a link between head posture and maxillary growth; the cited reviews address craniovertebral angle, pain and function. [2][3][9]

claims.claim: Forward head posture causes many problems throughout the body, and correct posture becomes natural with practice.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread cites an article on forward head posture and says it affects the whole body rather than just the face; one reply says good head posture 'becomes natural' after a while. [13]
claims.experts: A 2019 meta-analysis of cross-sectional studies found a head-posture difference between adults with and without neck pain but not in adolescents, and the authors describe the relationship as controversial. [9] A 2018 meta-analysis reported significant pooled effects of corrective exercise on craniovertebral angle and pain. [2] Posture change is described as needing repeated practice.

claims.claim: Fixing forward head posture can make the face look more recessed.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread title states that fixing forward head posture will make a person look more recessed in profile. [14]
claims.experts: No study cited here evaluates whether correcting forward head posture changes the apparent jawline, chin or profile. [9]
